title: Suphan Buri Food Guide 2026 — Fish Ball Noodles, Boat Noodles & Salee | ThailandAddict
metaDesc: What to eat in Suphan Buri, Thailand: bouncy fish ball noodles, tiny-bowl boat noodles, Tha Chin River fish, the famous Salee sponge cake, plus eats in the century-old Sam Chuk Market — with the spots locals actually go.
keywords: Suphan Buri food, Suphan Buri fish ball noodles, Suphan Buri boat noodles, Salee sponge cake Suphan Buri, Sam Chuk Market food, Tha Chin River fish
intro: Suphan Buri sits on the Tha Chin River and eats far better than a quiet province should. It is all about the noodles here — bouncy fish ball noodles and small-bowl boat noodles in a deep, rich broth — backed up by fresh Tha Chin River fish and capped off with Salee, the soft sponge cake everyone takes home. This is the food locals actually eat, and it is well worth the day trip.

blocks.html: Ask what Suphan Buri does best and the answer is "noodles" and "fish." The town sits right on the Tha Chin River, so freshwater fish is easy to come by and fish ball noodle shops are everywhere — walk a few hundred metres through the old town and you will pass several. Small-bowl boat noodles have been a snacking habit here for years too. We have picked the dishes that, once you try them, make it obvious why people drive out to Suphan Buri just to eat.

blocks.text: Fish Ball Noodles, Suphan Buri's Signature

blocks.html: Fish ball noodles are the dish this town is known for. The balls are made from freshwater fish like clown featherback and snakehead, ground and pounded in-house, so they come out springy and chewy with very little flour. Have them in a clear broth or tom yum. Many of the shops are in the old town and have been open for decades, and prices are still easy on the wallet.

items.name: Nai Bai Fish Ball Noodles
items.blurb: A legendary shop in the old town. The fish balls are blanched to order — firm and bouncy — in a clear, naturally sweet pork-bone broth. Locals treat this as the benchmark for the town's fish ball noodles. It gets packed at lunch.

items.name: Nai Phon Fish Ball Noodles
items.blurb: Another well-known name people keep asking about. The house-made fish balls are big and chewy, with thin and wide rice noodles plus egg noodles, and you can add shrimp wontons. The bold tom yum broth is a hit if you like things punchy.

items.name: Lao Jueng Fish Ball Noodles (Khrua Lao Jueng)
items.blurb: A long-running shop known for its fish balls and tom yum noodles. The tom yum broth is rich and well-balanced, the fish balls come out hot — soft but still springy. Reviewers praise it for being consistent.

items.name: Nai June Fish Ball Noodles
items.blurb: A plain, no-frills shop that regulars vouch for. Fresh fish balls, friendly prices, and a relaxed feel — good for breakfast before you head out for the day.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.html: A lot of the fish ball shops only sell from morning into the afternoon, and since the balls are made fresh daily they often sell out before evening. If you have a specific shop in mind, getting there before 2 pm is the safer bet — and order an extra bowl of fish balls on their own to taste the fish properly.

blocks.text: Boat Noodles, Small Bowls With Deep Broth

blocks.html: Boat noodles are an everyday snack in Suphan Buri — small bowls of thick, deeply flavoured broth with blood and offal or beef, topped with fried garlic and crispy pork crackling. Ordering several at once and stacking the empty bowls to show off is half the fun at the table. There are a handful of well-known shops in town to choose from.

items.name: May Boat Noodles, Suphan Buri Branch
items.blurb: A boat noodle shop that lands on review lists often. The broth is thick and fragrant with spices, the beef falls apart, and the small bowls keep you going. There are fish balls and offal to choose from — settle in for a long stack of bowls.

items.name: Thuk Pak Boat Noodles
items.blurb: A spot locals eat at regularly. The nam tok broth is well-balanced, the noodles are soft, and the pork crackling is freshly fried. Good value — you can order plenty of bowls without it stinging.

items.name: Dinosaur Boat Noodles
items.blurb: An oddly named shop in the Tha Rahat area where people stop for photos and a lively meal. Small bowls, deep broth, easy to order and easy on the budget — a handy stop on the way into town.

blocks.text: Tha Chin River Fish, the Local Staple

blocks.html: The Tha Chin River runs through Suphan Buri, which makes freshwater fish dishes the local specialty — grilled snakehead, snakehead baked in straw, fried clown featherback, even sheatfish fried with garlic. Riverside restaurants and the old-school places in town do these old-recipe fish dishes well, and they are perfect to order as a big shared meal with family.

items.name: Kui Mong
items.blurb: A legendary Chinese–Thai restaurant that has been part of Suphan Buri for over 90 years. Known for sheatfish fried with garlic and pepper, fried trahira, and salt-fried shrimp. Great for a family meal.

items.name: Samran Ocha (Sam Chuk Market)
items.blurb: An all-rounder for old-recipe river fish, now run by the second generation, in the Sam Chuk Market area. A good lunch stop after walking the market.

items.name: Riverside grilled-fish shops
items.blurb: Several shops in town and the surrounding districts do salt-grilled snakehead and snakehead baked in straw — juicy fish served with seafood dipping sauce and fresh vegetables.

blocks.title: Order fish the smart way
blocks.html: Grilled snakehead and the straw-baked version are two different things — the grilled one has that smoky, charred skin, while the straw-baked one is softer and juicier. If there are a few of you, order both and compare, then add fried clown featherback or garlic-fried sheatfish as another dish on the side.

Mention Suphan Buri souvenirs and the first thing that comes to mind is Salee — a light, soft, airy sponge cake with a lovely eggy aroma that has been tied to the town for ages. The big name, Ekachai Salee Suphan, opened around 1968 and earned a Shell Chuan Chim recommendation in 1980. These days there are several makers and plenty of flavours, from the original to pandan, even cute shapes like koi fish. It is easy to carry home and keeps for several days.

items: Ekachai Salee Suphan — the biggest maker, with several souvenir storefronts around town and lots of flavours and sizes. The easiest one for visitors to find.
Salee Mae Kim Liang — an original maker in the century-old Sam Chuk Market. The cake is soft and delicate, sold both boxed and in cute koi-fish shapes — handy to grab while you walk the market.
Salee Mae Buay — an old-school maker that older locals are attached to. Not too sweet, and another name people argue holds its own against the big brand.

blocks.text: Eating Around the Century-Old Sam Chuk Market

blocks.html: Sam Chuk is an old riverside market on the Tha Chin, more than a hundred years old. Shops start opening around 7–8 am and run until evening, with food — savoury and sweet — packed into narrow lanes you can graze through all morning. It makes for a self-contained eat-and-explore day trip.

items.name: Ja Choed Roast Duck
items.blurb: The market's legendary roast duck — crispy skin, tender meat, dressed in the shop's own sauce. People line up to take it home.

items.name: Jek Ao Wonton Noodles
items.blurb: A noodle shop that makes its own noodles, open in the market for over 70 years. Chewy noodles, plump shrimp wontons — an old favourite people come back for.

items.name: Yam Egg Noodles (old-style tom yum)
items.blurb: Old-style tom yum noodles in a thick, scant broth, eaten with a soft-boiled egg. Sweet-and-sour and well-balanced — a dish a lot of people love at the market.

items.name: Udom Chok Traditional Coffee
items.blurb: An old coffee shop in the market with a strong, traditional brew. Sip it in an old wooden room — a good break while you wander.

items.name: Old-Style Mooncakes & Chinese Sweets
items.blurb: The Heng and Liang Sun shops sell tightly filled mooncakes and old-style Chinese pastries — easy little gifts to carry away.

blocks.title: Make the most of Sam Chuk Market
blocks.html: The market is busiest on weekends, so going a little early means more on offer and fewer crowds. Many stalls only take cash, so bring small notes — and do not fill up at one shop, since the food is spread along the whole lane. Graze a bit at a time so you get through it all.

faq.q: What food should I try in Suphan Buri?
faq.a: Top of the list is fish ball noodles, made from springy freshwater fish, followed by small-bowl boat noodles in a deep, rich broth. Then there are Tha Chin River fish dishes like grilled snakehead and garlic-fried sheatfish, and the town's signature souvenir, the soft, airy Salee sponge cake.

faq.q: Where should I eat fish ball noodles in Suphan Buri?
faq.a: The shop locals treat as the benchmark is Nai Bai Fish Ball Noodles in the old town, followed by Nai Phon, Lao Jueng, and Nai June. The fish balls are made fresh daily and most shops are open from morning into the afternoon — go before 2 pm, as they tend to sell out fast.

faq.q: Where can I buy Salee cake in Suphan Buri?
faq.a: The biggest and easiest maker to find is Ekachai Salee Suphan, with several storefronts around town. For something more old-school, try Salee Mae Kim Liang in Sam Chuk Market, or Salee Mae Buay, which older locals are fond of.

faq.q: What is the food like at Sam Chuk Market, and what are the hours?
faq.a: Sam Chuk Market is open roughly 7–8 am until evening. Highlights include Ja Choed roast duck, Jek Ao's house-made wonton noodles, old-style tom yum yam egg noodles, Udom Chok traditional coffee, and old-school mooncakes and Chinese sweets. It is busiest on weekends.

faq.q: What Tha Chin River fish dishes are worth ordering?
faq.a: Popular ones are salt-grilled snakehead, juicy straw-baked snakehead, fried clown featherback, and sheatfish fried with garlic and pepper. Long-running spots like Kui Mong in town and Samran Ocha near Sam Chuk Market do old-recipe fish dishes well.
